comment: plain ASCII, the simplest interoperable address (some unit test frameworks let you record a reason, as in this comment)
case is preserved, not folded: the PRECIS IdentifierClass keeps upper and lower case distinct
all Latin, ø included; only the xn-- form of a domain is banned, the u-label is fine
an a-label (xn--...) is not permitted in the domain
an a-label is not permitted in the localpart either
an a-label is banned in any atom, not just the first
the ACE prefix is case-insensitive, so XN-- is an a-label too
one hyphen, not two: xn- is not the ACE prefix, so this is an ordinary localpart
U+200E LEFT-TO-RIGHT MARK is disallowed by PRECIS (unicode class Cf, precis C)
U+061C ARABIC LETTER MARK is disallowed by PRECIS (unicode class Cf, precis C)
U+200E and U+200F are bidi controls, disallowed by PRECIS

U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE in the localpart makes the address render as alice.aardvark@example.com; the real domain kravdraa.ec stays clean ASCII and aligns under DKIM/DMARC, but the override is class C, so the address is invalid
U+1F42A CAMEL is a symbol, not a letter or digit, so it is outside the permitted repertoire
U+3164 HANGUL FILLER renders as nothing, so this looks exactly like admin@example.com; the IdentifierClass disallows U+3164
the fullwidth letters ADMIN are compatibility forms, which the IdentifierClass disallows (to avoid ambiguity caused by nornalisation)
U+FE0F VARIATION SELECTOR-16 is invisible and changes nothing but the glyph chosen for 字

U+0640 ARABIC TATWEEL only elongates the preceding letter, so it gives one address an unbounded number of spellings; RFC5892 2.6 lists it as DISALLOWED although the category rules would have made it PVALID
the conjoining jamo render as 각, indistinguishable from the precomposed syllable below; the IdentifierClass disallows old Hangul jamo
the same syllable precomposed (U+AC01) is fine; Hangul with an ASCII domain is valid but, like Cyrillic, not interoperable
two non-ASCII scripts: U+0412 (В) is Cyrillic and ø is Latin
two non-ASCII scripts: 阿 is Han and ø is Latin
Cyrillic localpart with an ASCII domain is valid, but only Han (not Cyrillic) may be freely mixed with ASCII, so it is not interoperable
Han localpart with an ASCII domain is interoperable: Han may be combined with ASCII
Han plus ASCII (the Latin Q and example) is interoperable
all Han plus the ASCII dot: a single non-ASCII script is interoperable
ASCII localpart with a single-script (Han) domain is interoperable
all Devanagari, including its combining vowel signs: a single script is interoperable
Latin localpart (ø) with an ASCII domain: one script, interoperable
Arabic (U+0627) with ASCII digits: the only left-to-right code points are digits, which is allowed
Arabic (U+0627, right-to-left) mixed with left-to-right letters is valid but not interoperable
café in NFC (precomposed U+00E9) is interoperable
the same café in NFD (e + U+0301 combining acute), one code point longer; valid, but not interoperable because it is not NFC
two ASCII dots are valid code points, but WHATWG type=email forbids the empty atoms
a quoted-string localpart is valid RFC5322 and uses only ASCII, but WHATWG type=email has no quoting, so it is not interoperable
SPACE (U+0020) is permitted, so a quoted-string may contain one; WHATWG type=email has no quoting, so this is not interoperable either

seven different banned code points follow the å: U+0009 TAB, U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE, U+FEFF ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE, U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN, U+00A0 NO-BREAK SPACE, U+2003 EM SPACE and U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE; U+0020 is the only one of these rule 2 admits
U+00B7 between two l's is the Catalan ela geminada, permitted in context (RFC5892 A.3)
U+00B7 is only permitted between two l's (RFC5892 A.3); here it is not
Arabic-Indic (U+0660) and Extended Arabic-Indic (U+06F0) digits must not be mixed (RFC5892 A.8 and A.9)
